rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses is again swayed by kinship with the Israelite, whom he and the Israelite see as their common enemy.
rows.anchor: swayed once again by his feeling of kinship with the Israelite

words: مَا عَلِمْتُ لَكُم مِّنْ إِلَٰهٍ غَيْرِى
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's assertion is not literal: although Egyptians worshipped many gods, Pharaoh was regarded as divine incarnation and received adoration as Lord All-Highest.
rows.anchor: ancient Egyptians worshipped many gods, this observation is not to be taken literally

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As an alternative, ittali'u can mean to ascend to the god of Moses.
rows.anchor: Or: "ascend to the god of Moses".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lofty tower evokes pyramid building and derisively mocks Moses' conception of God as an all-embracing power beyond all existence.
rows.anchor: a derisory, contemptuous reference to Moses' concept of God as an all-embracing Power, inconceivably high above all that exists

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase refers to the beings or powers whom the audience treated as God's partners.
rows.anchor: Lit., "those (God-)partners of yours": see note 64 above.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sentence structure shows that even a follower of a great apostle can sin through pride and self-exaltation, exemplifying the preceding passage's false imagery.
rows.anchor: a person who had been a follower of one of the greatest of God's apostles was not above the possibility of sinning under

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad rejects the conventional identification of Qarun with biblical Korah as unwarranted; the account teaches a moral lesson rather than recounting history.
rows.anchor: The conventional "identification" of Qarun with the Korah of the Old Testament

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says Qarun's moral role explains why the Qur'an juxtaposes him with Pharaoh, the arch-sinner.
rows.anchor: the juxtaposition, elsewhere in the Qur'an (29:39 and 40:24), of Qarun with Pharaoh, the arch-sinner

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Usbah means a group of ten or more, up to forty; metonymically it conveys the great weight of Qarun's treasure-chests.
rows.anchor: The term 'usbah denotes a company of ten or more (up to forty) persons

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mafatih can mean keys or what is locked away; the context requires the latter sense, treasure-chests.
rows.anchor: The noun mafatih is a plural of both miftah or miftah ("key") and maftah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking the hereafter through God's gifts means spending in charity and on good causes.
rows.anchor: I.e., by spending in charity and on good causes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call not to neglect one's share in worldly life asks for generosity balanced by moderation.
rows.anchor: a call to generosity and, at the same time, to moderation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qarun claims his wealth came from his own experience, shrewdness, and ability.
rows.anchor: as a result of my own experience, shrewdness and ability

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sinners are generally blind to their failings and consequently do not respond to admonition.
rows.anchor: are, as a rule, blind to their own failings and, therefore, not responsive to admonition

words: فَمَا كَانَ لَهُۥ مِن فِئَةٍۢ يَنصُرُونَهُۥ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally says Qarun had no host at all to aid him.
rows.anchor: Lit., "he had no host whatever to succour him ... , etc.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad allows that the earth swallowing Qarun may metaphorically describe a sudden catastrophic loss of all his wealth and former grandeur.
rows.anchor: may possibly be a metaphor of a catastrophic, unforeseen loss - from whatever cause - of all his worldly goods

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal wording is 'you create a lie.'
rows.anchor: Lit., "you create a lie".

rows.speaker: Baghawi and Zamakhshari (on Al-Hasan's authority)
rows.claim: Baghawi and Zamakhshari, citing Al-Hasan, advance the reading that the phrase means cutting across the way of nature.
rows.anchor: advanced by Baghawi and (on the authority of Al-Hasan) by Zamakhshari

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi adopts the same interpretation exclusively and without reservation.
rows.anchor: Razi adopts it exclusively and without reservation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If verses 45-46 address believers generally, as the plural forms suggest, the phrase means whatever of the divine writ has revealed itself to the reader's understanding.
rows.anchor: the above phrase may be taken to mean "whatever of the divine writ has revealed itself to thy understanding"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God brings human beings forth anew; Asad links this to 10:4 and notes a more general formulation at 30:27.
rows.anchor: cf. 10:4 and the corresponding note 8. (A more general formulation of the same statement is found in verse 27 of this surah.)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to note 4 on 13:2 for his discussion of the heavens' supports.
rows.anchor: See note 4 on 13:2.

words: وَأَلْقَى فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ رَوَٰسِىَ أَن تَمِيدَ بِكُمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to note 11 on 16:15 for his explanation of the mountains that keep the earth from swaying.
rows.anchor: See note 11 on 16:15.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift in the divine pronoun from 'He' to 'We' signals that infinite God cannot be contained by pronouns for finite created beings; pronouns accommodate human language.
rows.anchor: the personal pronoun relating to God is suddenly changed - in this instance, from "He" to "We" - in order

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses the phrase literally as 'thereon' and takes zawj to mean a kind, as in 26:7.
rows.anchor: Lit., "thereon". As in 26:7, the term zawi has here the significance of "a kind".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here 'the evildoers' are those who attribute divine powers to beings or things other than God.
rows.anchor: Sc., "who ascribe divine powers to beings or things other than God".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders latif as 'unfathomable' and refers readers to his discussion in note 89 on surah 6.
rows.anchor: For my rendering of latif as "unfathomable", see surah 6, note 89.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People give the answer that God created everything from vague habit, without seeing that acknowledging Him as ultimate cause logically requires surrender to Him alone.
rows.anchor: a cognition of God as the Ultimate Cause of all existence logically postulates one's full surrender to Him, and to Him alone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad compares the description of God's inexhaustible words with a similar passage at 18:109.
rows.anchor: Cf. a similar passage in 18:109.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For God's power, creating and resurrecting many people is no different from doing so for one; every soul is as fully within His knowledge as all mankind.
rows.anchor: there is no difference between the creation and resurrection of many and of one

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-adna literally means 'nearer' and here refers to suffering in this world; Asad points to his note on 52:47.
rows.anchor: Lit., "nearer", i:e., in this world: for an explanation, see note 27 on 52:47.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means that they might return to righteousness.
rows.anchor: Lit., "so that they might return [to righteousness]".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naming adopted children by their real fathers makes their adoptive relationship clear and safeguards their true identity.
rows.anchor: make it clear that your relationship is an adoptive one, and do not create the impression that they are your real children

words: وَلَيْسَ عَلَيْكُمْ جُنَاحٌۭ فِيمَآ أَخْطَأْتُم بِهِۦ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The excused mistake includes misattributing a child's parentage or affectionately calling the child one's son or daughter.
rows.anchor: by making a mistake in the attribution of the child's parentage, or by calling him or her, out of love, "my son" or "my daughter"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad refers readers to note 49 on 10:31 for the opening question about who provides sustenance.
rows.anchor: See note 49 on the first sentence of 10:31.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: False objects of worship, including saints, angels, relics, fetishes, and deified natural forces, will disown their worshippers on Resurrection Day; this symbolizes humanity's final perception of ultimate reality.
rows.anchor: will 'bear witness" against their one-time worshippers on Resurrection Day, and will "disown" them
